paragraphs: This paper investigates why image generators using discrete representations often trail systems using continuous representations. Its central finding is that the gap comes mainly from how many bits the compressed image representation contains. In the authors’ investigation, enlarging the discrete codebook closes that gap, allowing discrete tokenizers to match or exceed continuous alternatives.

A larger codebook creates another problem: existing discrete generation methods can become expensive to train or lose performance. BAR addresses this by generating each token through its constituent bits. An autoregressive transformer uses a masked bit prediction head to progressively construct tokens, giving the framework a way to support arbitrary codebook sizes.

On ImageNet-256, BAR reports a state-of-the-art gFID of 0.99, alongside reduced sampling costs and faster convergence than prior continuous approaches. The result connects representation capacity with a generation method capable of using it: allocating more bits helps, and predicting those bits progressively makes the larger discrete representation practical.
icml-2026-autoregressive-image-generatio.tldr: BAR generates image tokens progressively through their bits, enabling larger discrete codebooks and reporting state-of-the-art ImageNet-256 generation quality.

paragraphs: A text-attributed graph describes its nodes through both written content and connections. Those two information sources can disagree, and each can contain noise. The paper argues that forcing them together too rigidly leaves their representations misaligned and can spread interference as information moves through the graph.

UDPD starts by learning separate representations of node meaning and graph structure. It then uses two parallel diffusion branches that guide one another, progressively aligning the representations while removing noise. This preserves a distinction between the two sources during the process of bringing them together.

The strength of that interaction depends on uncertainty at each node. During the reverse diffusion process, uncertainty adjusts how strongly the branches influence one another, making their coupling adaptive rather than fixed. Experiments on five public benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a coordinated approach to two linked problems: reconciling different information sources and preventing their noise from being amplified during integration.
icml-2026-bridging-structure-and-semanti.tldr: UDPD uses uncertainty to control interaction between semantic and structural diffusion branches, improving text-attributed graph representations on five benchmarks.

paragraphs: Errors in multi-agent systems can travel across agents, tools, and lengthy reasoning sequences. This makes identifying the responsible step difficult, even when a failure began with a small mistake. CORRECT builds on the observation that different-looking execution logs often contain recurring structural patterns of failure.

The framework stores condensed descriptions of those patterns in an online cache. When a new request produces a trajectory to inspect, an LLM can reuse relevant cached knowledge to target its search for the error. This transfers experience without retraining, with the abstract reporting adaptation to changing deployments in subseconds.

The authors also introduce CORRECT-Error, containing more than 2,000 annotated trajectories. Its error-injection process is guided by real-world distributions, and human evaluation checks alignment with natural failures. Across seven multi-agent applications, CORRECT improves step-level error localization by up to 19.8% over existing approaches with near-zero overhead. These findings support reusing compact failure structures as a practical way to improve automated debugging.
icml-2026-correct-condensed-error-recogn.tldr: CORRECT reuses cached failure patterns to locate errors in multi-agent systems without retraining, improving localization by up to 19.8%.

paragraphs: DocHop tests whether a model can combine document text with evidence from several charts. Reading chart values alone is insufficient: the surrounding narrative determines which entities matter and how their values should be combined. This targets a capability that benchmarks evaluating charts and documents separately leave underexplored.

Each question refers to a semantic label defined in the narrative. A model must interpret that label, resolve the relevant entities, follow multiple constraints, and aggregate the corresponding chart evidence. The benchmark uses a randomized generation process that establishes the logic first, allowing the authors to control reasoning depth and visual density across 2,074 examples in six task categories.

Human annotators exceed 90% accuracy, while the best evaluated model reaches 62.83%. Models enhanced for reasoning perform better, but accuracy declines as the reasoning becomes more complex. The findings expose a substantial gap in connecting textual instructions to visual evidence through multiple steps, even among models with strong performance on other structured visual tasks.
icml-2026-dochop-benchmarking-out-of-dom.tldr: DocHop reveals a substantial human–model gap when document text determines how evidence from multiple charts must be interpreted and combined.

paragraphs: The paper develops a network for predicting Hamiltonian matrices, with the aim of accelerating electronic structure calculations. These predictions need to respect rotations: rotating a molecular structure should transform the predicted matrix consistently. Enforcing this global three-dimensional rotational symmetry can involve costly mathematical operations.

QHNetV2 uses the relationship between off-diagonal matrix blocks and local coordinate frames to simplify the computation. It performs off-diagonal feature updates and message passing through operations that respect SO(2) symmetry within those frames. Together, these operations maintain global SO(3) equivariance without using the expensive SO(3) Clebsch–Gordan tensor products. A continuous SO(2) tensor product also combines features at each node.

Experiments on QH9 and MD17 report superior performance across varied molecular structures and trajectories, supporting the model’s generalization within those evaluations. The methodological contribution is a more efficient route to symmetry-aware prediction: carefully chosen local operations can preserve the required global rotational behavior while avoiding a costly component of earlier computation.
icml-2026-efficient-prediction-of-so-3-e.tldr: QHNetV2 predicts rotationally consistent Hamiltonian matrices using efficient local-frame operations and reports strong performance on molecular datasets.

paragraphs: This study examines AI grading on real handwritten calculus work from the University of California, Irvine. Its motivation is practical: large undergraduate courses create heavy grading workloads, often leaving students with little feedback. The empirical analysis covers thousands of in-person, proctored quiz submissions from nearly 800 students.

The system combines optical character recognition with language models prompted to follow structured grading rubrics. It produces both scores and formative feedback. Because the setting has no single definitive ground-truth grade, the researchers evaluate it from several perspectives: official teaching-assistant scores, student surveys, and independent human review.

The study finds strong agreement with teaching-assistant scoring, while a large majority of generated feedback is judged correct or acceptable across quizzes. It also examines failure modes and develops rubric and prompt-design principles. The evaluation framework addresses the combined challenges of reading handwriting, reasoning about mathematics, and assigning partial credit. A standardized benchmark is presented as a future direction built on this work.
icml-2026-evaluating-ai-grading-on-real-.tldr: A large study of handwritten calculus grading finds strong agreement with teaching assistants and broadly acceptable feedback using rubric-guided language models.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups samples using several representations of the same data. Anchor-based methods summarize those samples through representative points, but conventional approaches implicitly distribute anchors uniformly across clusters. The paper argues that this can underrepresent larger clusters, which may need more anchors to capture their internal structure.

FCFMVC encourages anchor allocation to reflect cluster proportions through two connected paths. One uses a bipartite graph to connect anchor allocation with discrete sample assignments, then feeds cluster size and dispersion back into anchor assignment. The other treats anchors as pseudo-samples and directly constrains how many belong to each cluster within a tolerance margin.

Alignment between anchor and sample labels couples the two paths, connecting detailed anchor decisions with broader cluster organization. Here, the allocation concern centers on cluster size and structure. The authors report linear time and space costs for the optimization, supporting scalability, and experiments across datasets of different sizes demonstrate effectiveness. The approach makes representational resources responsive to unequal cluster needs.
icml-2026-fine-to-coarse-fairness-inform.tldr: FCFMVC allocates clustering anchors according to cluster size and structure, improving representation while retaining linear time and space costs.

paragraphs: An LLM workflow coordinates several model or agent calls to complete a task. Designing both the arrangement of those calls and their individual prompts often requires substantial human effort. FlowBot studies how to learn these workflows from data, treating their construction as an optimization problem with two connected levels.

The outer optimization loop changes a high-level sketch describing how the calls should be organized. The inner loop improves the individual calls one at a time. Both use textual gradients: feedback expressed in language to guide revisions. Within the inner loop, that feedback is passed backward through the workflow layer by layer so components can be improved modularly.

The discovered workflows perform competitively against strong baselines using human-crafted or generated workflows. That finding supports automated workflow induction as a viable approach, without claiming that it consistently beats those alternatives. The distinctive idea is to optimize the overall arrangement and its local components together, giving data-driven feedback a role at both levels of system design.
icml-2026-flowbot-inducing-llm-workflows.tldr: FlowBot learns LLM workflow structures and individual calls through nested optimization with textual feedback, achieving competitive performance against strong baselines.

paragraphs: Reasoning about causes across images requires identifying relevant variables and understanding what changes when an intervention occurs. The paper addresses the brittleness of vision-language models on these tasks, especially intervention and counterfactual questions. It argues that causal guidance supplied only through text prompts leaves the mechanisms outside the model’s execution.

BridgeVLM first infers a causal graph from multiple images. It converts that graph into structured Causal Tokens, which added RAMP layers process inside the language-model decoder through causal message passing. A training interface called M3S combines fine-grained supervision at local and global levels, connecting the learned structure with the model’s reasoning process.

On CausalVLBench intervention tasks, BridgeVLM reaches 54.4% accuracy compared with 33.2% using prompt-level supervision. Results on Causal3D rise from 43.6% to 49.0%, while causal structure learning on CausalVLBench improves from 33.4% to 75.1% F1. These results support integrating causal structure into model execution as a useful approach to the evaluated multi-image reasoning tasks.
icml-2026-from-prompts-to-tokens-interna.tldr: BridgeVLM embeds causal graphs into decoder execution through structured tokens, improving multi-image intervention reasoning and causal structure learning.

paragraphs: Geometric Flow Grounding addresses a problem in learning dynamics from observations: a model can mix up what a state represents with how it is moving. Over time, its predicted trajectory may leave the geometric structure learned from the data. The framework separates state representation from motion to constrain that evolution.

Its differentiable Neural Tangent Projection Layer restricts dynamics to tangent directions of the learned data manifold. These are directions compatible with the local geometry of that representation. The same projection also produces a residual measuring the component inconsistent with the allowed motion, giving the framework a signal for verification as well as prediction.

The reported applications include reduced numerical aliasing and better long-horizon stability in sparse dynamical systems, plus recovery of interpretable gene regulatory motifs from single-cell data. For deepfake detection, the projection residual serves as a zero-shot measure of inconsistency with pretrained world-model flows. Together, these applications demonstrate how one geometric operation can support both discovering dynamics and checking synthetic content.
icml-2026-geometric-flow-grounding-a-uni.tldr: Geometric Flow Grounding constrains learned motion to manifold-compatible directions, supporting dynamics discovery and zero-shot deepfake detection.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning allows clients to learn collectively as their data changes, even when earlier data cannot be stored. Replay methods address this constraint by generating synthetic examples. GFedCL focuses on information that existing replay approaches overlook: differences across clients or locations and changes over time.

The method constructs relational graphs that capture both spatial and temporal relationships, using attention mechanisms to represent their relevance. It combines those graphs with generative adversarial learning to produce synthetic data. The intended benefit is replay that reflects how distributed data sources relate and evolve, making those relationships part of the generation process.

The abstract states that GFedCL can generate data matching the expectation of the real distribution while providing theoretical privacy guarantees. This is an expectation-matching claim, rather than a claim of exact distributional identity. The reported experiments consistently outperform state-of-the-art federated continual learning methods, including a 27.95% improvement on TinyImageNet. These findings support incorporating spatial and temporal context into synthetic replay.
icml-2026-gfedcl-graph-based-federated-c.tldr: GFedCL uses spatial and temporal relationship graphs to improve privacy-preserving synthetic replay for federated continual learning.

paragraphs: Successor representations separate predictions about future dynamics from rewards, which helps an agent adapt when rewards change. Their weakness is dependence on the policy used to generate those predictions. Changing behavior can make the representation obsolete, while complex environment layouts can produce dense, overlapping features that scale poorly.

The Hierarchical Successor Representation introduces temporal abstractions into predictive representations. This produces state features that are robust to task-induced policy changes. Applying non-negative matrix factorization then compresses these features into a sparse, low-rank representation, giving the agent a more compact basis for transferring knowledge between tasks.

In environments with multiple compartments, the resulting HSR-NMF representation supports highly sample-efficient transfer to new tasks and reveals interpretable topological structure. The authors describe it as a policy-agnostic hierarchical map combining model-free optimality with model-based flexibility. They also show that its temporally extended predictions can guide exploration in large, procedurally generated environments. The contribution therefore spans both reusing learned structure and exploring unfamiliar spaces.
icml-2026-hierarchical-successor-represe.tldr: Hierarchical successor representations learn compact environmental structure that supports robust task transfer and exploration despite task-induced policy changes.

paragraphs: GFlowNets have been used to improve recommendation diversity and reduce popularity bias, but offline recommendation creates a particular obstacle. Training is restricted to a fixed log of examples, which covers only some possible token transitions. An objective designed around online-style assumptions can assign probability to transitions unsupported by that log.

The paper formalizes why applying Sub-Trajectory Balance directly becomes non-identifiable: the available evidence does not uniquely determine the learned flows. It identifies flow overestimation, forward probability leakage, and backward compensation as three mechanisms behind the mismatch. CFlower adds a conservative penalty on unsupported forward flow and constrains policy learning to the token-prefix graph induced by the dataset.

Training samples from the current policy within that supported graph, respecting the offline setting. On three Amazon recommendation datasets, CFlower improves distributional matching and the trade-off between accuracy and exposure relative to prior GFlowNet and supervised fine-tuning baselines. It also provides a more reliable reference policy for subsequent reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.
icml-2026-improving-llm-based-recommende.tldr: CFlower constrains offline GFlowNet recommendation learning to logged-data support, improving distributional matching and the accuracy–exposure trade-off.

paragraphs: This paper connects three observed properties of learned representations: generalization performance, similarity between different models, and similarity to human neural activity. It finds that models with stronger generalization also align more closely with brain activity, and that all three properties are significantly correlated with one another.

The proposed common descriptor is local intrinsic dimension: how many dimensions are needed to characterize the representation in a local neighborhood. Lower local dimension is consistently associated with better generalization and stronger alignment, both across models and between models and brains. Measures of global dimension fail to capture the same relationships.

The authors also find that increasing model capacity and training-data scale systematically lowers local intrinsic dimension. This provides a geometric account of the observed benefits of scaling and the convergence of learned representations. The evidence establishes associations and a useful descriptive property; the stated findings do not make reducing local dimension alone a demonstrated intervention for improving generalization or reproducing human neural processing.
icml-2026-local-intrinsic-dimension-of-r.tldr: Lower local intrinsic dimension is associated with better generalization and stronger representational alignment across AI models and human brain activity.

paragraphs: Anchors explains individual model predictions through rules, but generating those explanations can be computationally expensive. Its search gradually refines a rule until it is precise enough for a particular input. MAnchors takes advantage of that iterative process by retaining useful intermediate rules from earlier explanations.

The memory stores rules with broad coverage but initially low precision. For a new input, a horizontal transformation replaces features in a retrieved rule to make it applicable. A vertical transformation then refines the adapted rule until it reaches sufficient precision. This separates the task of fitting a rule to the current input from making that rule reliably explanatory.

Evaluations across tabular, text, and image datasets show significantly shorter explanation-generation times while maintaining fidelity and understandability. The practical significance is that prior explanation work can become reusable material for later requests. Broad intermediate rules serve as starting points, while input-specific refinement preserves the quality needed for the final explanation in time-sensitive applications.
icml-2026-manchors-memorization-based-ac.tldr: MAnchors accelerates rule-based explanations by adapting and refining remembered intermediate rules while maintaining fidelity and understandability.

paragraphs: Fast optimization guarantees often depend on smoothness assumptions that control how rapidly gradients change. Recent generalizations allow this control to vary with gradient magnitude, accommodating more objectives, but their guarantees have largely been restricted to Euclidean geometry. This paper extends the analysis to the more general geometries used by mirror descent.

The authors introduce an ℓ*-smoothness condition that measures Hessian size using a general norm and its dual. A central proof tool is a generalized self-bounding property: controlling the gap from an objective’s optimal value can also control gradient size. This relationship supports convergence analysis without reverting to the usual Euclidean smoothness framework.

Under the proposed conditions, mirror-descent-type algorithms match convergence rates available under classical smoothness. The paper also establishes sharp stochastic mirror-descent guarantees and extends its theory to non-convex and composite optimization. The implications for LLM pretraining and post-training are presented as possible practical relevance of the theory, rather than as reported training experiments or established performance improvements.
icml-2026-mirror-descent-under-generaliz.tldr: A generalized smoothness condition extends mirror-descent convergence guarantees beyond Euclidean geometry while matching classical smoothness rates.

paragraphs: Inferring molecular structure from several spectroscopic measurements requires combining signals with different information characteristics. The paper finds that simply concatenating spectral sequences can degrade performance because heterogeneous modalities become imbalanced. MM-Spectrum addresses this with a sparse mixture-of-experts model designed specifically for multispectral inputs.

Its routing mechanism receives both token content and the identity of the spectral modality. This lets routing account explicitly for where a signal comes from. The framework also includes shared and interaction experts with different capacities, aiming to capture information specific to individual modalities as well as useful combinations across them.

These design choices seek to preserve complementary evidence while suppressing interference caused by noise. The authors report consistent, substantial improvements when all modalities are present, when two are available, and when modalities are missing. Ablation studies and interpretability analyses support the findings. The contribution is a way to make expert allocation sensitive to spectral differences while still learning the cross-modal relationships needed for molecular structure inference.
icml-2026-mm-spectrum-multimodal-multi-s.tldr: MM-Spectrum uses modality-aware expert routing to integrate heterogeneous spectra and improve molecular structure inference across differing modality availability.

paragraphs: Representation intervention aims to steer language-model behavior through internal representations without changing the underlying model weights. This paper finds that applying the same correction to every input can damage general capabilities on benign requests. Different samples need different correction directions and strengths, and some inputs should not receive an intervention.

MARI addresses those decisions through specialized adapters and an energy-based gate. The adapters compete to capture nonlinear correction patterns and determine how to steer each sample. The gate uses internal propagation dynamics to identify inputs for which intervention is applicable, adding an adaptive decision about whether correction is appropriate.

Experiments across multiple model families and sizes report state-of-the-art alignment performance. MARI improves results on TruthfulQA, BBQ, and safety benchmarks while maintaining or improving performance on general tasks including MMLU and ARC. These findings support making both the form and applicability of intervention responsive to the input, allowing behavioral alignment to coexist with preserved general capabilities in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-multi-adapter-representation-i.tldr: MARI adapts when and how to intervene in language-model representations, improving alignment while preserving or improving evaluated general capabilities.

paragraphs: Language models commonly receive tool documentation and examples in their context before calling external interfaces. This adds inference overhead, and longer contexts can increase hallucination risks. ParaTool aims to internalize the details of tools in dedicated parameter modules so tool calling does not depend on supplying those documents and examples at inference.

The framework has three stages. Tool pretraining encodes each tool’s knowledge into an independent, loadable parameter module. A gating network then performs soft selection, weighing and combining relevant modules dynamically. Finally, joint fine-tuning updates the tool parameters to bring training and inference behavior into alignment.

Experiments on Stable ToolBench and BFCL show significant improvements over strong in-context-learning baselines while reducing computational complexity. The contribution goes beyond training general tool-use ability: it explicitly represents tool-specific knowledge in modules that the model can integrate as needed. The reported findings support parameterized tool representations as an alternative means of providing the detailed interface knowledge required for successful calls.
icml-2026-paratool-shifting-tool-represe.tldr: ParaTool stores tool knowledge in dynamically combined parameter modules, improving tool calling while reducing reliance on lengthy in-context documentation.

paragraphs: EEG foundation models seek representations that transfer across tasks, but their recordings contain substantial high-frequency noise and differences between people. Reconstructing the raw waveform can make pretraining sensitive to random fluctuations. PATCHCODE changes the supervision signal while keeping the encoder’s input as continuous EEG patches.

The method combines two levels of predictive learning. It predicts missing patch representations to retain fine spatial and temporal structure, while also aligning those predictions with region-aware discrete codes from a frozen tokenizer. The discrete targets are intended to provide stable semantic anchors alongside the more detailed patch-level objective.

Experiments cover sixteen downstream datasets spanning emotion recognition, motor imagery, sleep staging, seizure detection, vigilance, stress, and clinical diagnosis. PATCHCODE is competitive with state-of-the-art baselines and shows notable data-efficiency gains when labels are limited. The findings support combining continuous signal processing with discrete supervision, so transferable representations can retain detailed EEG structure while learning from targets designed to be more stable than waveform reconstruction alone.
icml-2026-patchcode-discrete-latent-pred.tldr: PATCHCODE combines continuous EEG inputs with discrete predictive targets, achieving competitive transfer performance and gains when labeled data is scarce.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits whose reward-based parameter estimates can be updated only occasionally. It distinguishes this restriction from strict batching: a learner can still observe contexts and choose actions sequentially between updates. Some batched methods additionally prevent decisions from adapting to the sequence of contexts and actions within an interval.

The authors propose two algorithms requiring only O(log log T) parameter updates over T rounds. BLCE-G uses a static update schedule and achieves minimax-optimal regret, up to polylogarithmic factors in T, in both small- and large-action-set regimes. Regret measures the performance lost through the learner’s decisions relative to the comparison policy.

BLCE removes a near G-optimal design step that is a major computational bottleneck in prior strictly batched static-grid methods. It preserves minimax-optimal regret and achieves the lowest known runtime complexity among optimal algorithms. The paper also extends the principles to generalized linear contextual bandits with near-optimal guarantees. The results show how rare parameter updates can coexist with computational efficiency and strong decision-quality guarantees.
icml-2026-practical-and-optimal-algorith.tldr: Two contextual-bandit algorithms achieve optimal regret guarantees with very few parameter updates, while BLCE removes a major computational bottleneck.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how weather-model validation loss changes with model size, training-data size, and available computation. Its goal is to identify efficient ways to improve forecasting models. The analysis is empirical, comparing scaling behavior across a range of models and examining how a fixed compute budget should be allocated.

Aurora shows the strongest response to additional data: a tenfold increase in the training dataset reduces validation loss by up to a factor of 3.2. GraphCast offers the greatest parameter efficiency, but limited hardware utilization complicates that advantage. These findings distinguish obtaining useful performance from each parameter from using computing hardware effectively.

Under fixed compute budgets, the analysis favors allocating resources to more total training data over increasing model size. It also finds that weather models consistently benefit more from width than depth in the studied settings, a pattern differing from language-model scaling. The results suggest prioritizing wider architectures and larger effective training datasets when designing future weather models.
icml-2026-scaling-laws-of-global-weather.tldr: Empirical weather-model scaling favors more training data and wider architectures, with distinct trade-offs between parameter efficiency and hardware utilization.

paragraphs: Security feedback often arrives only after a complete program has been generated. That is a poor fit for interactive coding, where developers or models may need to assess an unfinished prefix. SecCodePRM assigns context-aware security scores at individual steps along a code trajectory, making feedback available throughout generation.

Training labels come from static analyzers and expert annotations. Their step-level granularity helps the model focus on regions associated with vulnerabilities spanning procedure boundaries. For vulnerability detection, the system combines scores in a risk-sensitive way that emphasizes dangerous steps. For generation, it ranks candidate continuations and favors those with higher cumulative reward.

The paper evaluates full-code detection, partial-code detection, and secure code generation, reporting improvements over prior approaches in all three settings while preserving functional correctness. These results suggest that denser security feedback can improve the evaluated security outcomes without sacrificing utility. The same scoring model supports both diagnosing code and selecting continuations, connecting detection directly to the generation process.
icml-2026-seccodeprm-a-process-reward-mo.tldr: SecCodePRM scores security throughout code generation, improving vulnerability detection and secure continuation selection while preserving evaluated functional correctness.

paragraphs: Progressive learning saves pretraining computation by beginning with a smaller model and expanding it during training. This paper focuses on increasing width partway through training, where instability makes expansion difficult. The authors find that naive initialization disrupts activation statistics and causes loss spikes, while copying existing components creates gradient symmetry that restricts feature diversity.

SPARKLING addresses these two problems separately. RMS-scale consistency preserves the scale of signals during expansion, stabilizing activation statistics. Asymmetric resets of optimizer state and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup break the symmetry that would otherwise make copied components learn too similarly.

Experiments on dense and mixture-of-experts models cover multiple width dimensions and optimizer families. SPARKLING consistently outperforms training from scratch in those experiments and reduces training cost by up to 35% when doubling width. The findings show why successful expansion needs both continuity and differentiation: the enlarged model must preserve useful signal behavior while allowing its additional capacity to develop diverse features.
icml-2026-sparkling-balancing-signal-pre.tldr: SPARKLING stabilizes mid-training width expansion while encouraging feature diversity, reducing training cost by up to 35% under doubled width.

paragraphs: Spectral methods can solve low-dimensional partial differential equations very accurately, but their computational burden grows sharply with dimension. Sparse-grid and related techniques extend their usefulness into moderate dimensions. Physics-informed neural networks offer a route to higher dimensions, although accuracy and efficiency can remain problematic.

Spectral-informed neural networks combine these approaches by working directly with spectral representations. This avoids spatial derivative computations and reduces memory consumption. The paper introduces Modified SINNs, adding coefficient-decay scaling and basis embeddings motivated by harmonic analysis. These changes are designed to improve high-dimensional accuracy and help approximate spectral coefficients that are unknown.

Numerical experiments include both steady and time-dependent equations. Modified SINNs outperform sparse-grid spectral methods on middle-dimensional problems when spectral information is incomplete, and outperform PINNs in accuracy on high-dimensional problems. Those are distinct comparisons under stated settings. The contribution is a refined spectral-domain learning method that makes use of spectral structure while addressing situations where conventional spectral computation or neural PDE solvers face difficulties.
icml-2026-spectral-informed-neural-netwo.tldr: Modified SINNs improve spectral-domain PDE learning, outperforming sparse-grid methods with incomplete spectral information and PINNs on high-dimensional accuracy.
